title: Same orbits, different rocket dreams? China, India, and the case for global space security studies
summary: Argues for global space security studies using China and India as entry point.
abstract: This article puts forward the case for a global space security studies using China and India as an entry point. Recent trends, including the militarization and commercialization of outer space, growing concerns over orbital debris, and the expanding number of state and non-state actors engaged in space activities, have renewed scholarly and policy debates over the nature and scope of contemporary space security. However, although the participation of new actors, particularly from the Global South, has introduced greater diversity and plurality in understandings of what constitutes space security, prevailing analyses remain largely couched in Eurocentrism. This results in reifying a universal understanding of space security rooted in Western strategic cultures, experience, and production of knowledge, which often distorts or obscures the different meanings, referent objects, and drivers of security policy in non-Western contexts. Using the cases of China and India, this article shows the ways in which their understandings and practices of space security are hybrid, influenced by an amalgam of domestic and international factors. This requires going beyond looking at how China and India’s approaches to space security resemble the Eurocentric concept of space security, which offers an incomplete and distorting view. It also entails considering how their concept of space security is defined by differences that are glossed over by Eurocentric assumptions. In so doing, this article

title: Satellite Ownership and Sustainable Space Exploration: Responsibility-Embedded Polycentric Governance Model (RE-PGM)
summary: Proposes a responsibility-embedded polycentric governance model for satellite ownership and orbital congestion.
abstract: Abstract. The accelerated development and increased reliance on satellite infrastructure have spurred concerns related to orbital congestion, space debris, and the long-term sustainability of outer space. Although previous studies have approached the problem of space sustainability from a technological, economic, or international law point of view, they tend to isolate a specific dimension of the problem and lack exploratory capacity in proposing solutions. In particular, there has been a significant gap in research focusing on the problem of satellite ownership in relation to space sustainability. This study posits that satellite ownership structure is a key variable for space sustainability as the increased number of commercial players present a challenge for accountability, monitoring and transparency. The study contributes to the scholarship in two ways. Empirically, it conducts an extensive quantitative and qualitative analysis to understand who owns the satellites (state/ companies), what is their purpose and technological design. Theoretically, the study advances the scholarship by proposing Responsibility-Embedded Polycentric Governance Model, grounded in 7 adapted principles, 2 space science communication mechanisms and 2 economic principles the Precautionary Principle and the Polluter Pays Principles. The study further highlights the crucial role of science communications along with transparent, open-access data and participation of wide range of stakeholders.

title: Satellite launch traffic forecast based on the global Gross Domestic Product and constellation plans
summary: Forecasts satellite launch traffic from global GDP and constellation plans as input to debris models.
abstract: Satellite launch traffic is an important input into space debris evolutionary models. Slight variations in launch traffic can have a large impact on the space landscape as a whole, since the number of satellites in orbit directly influences collision risk. In recent years the trend has been going towards employing satellite constellations such as Starlink. Information about planned constellations is publicly available and is used in this work to predict the future launch traffic. The 8 largest constellations launched so far and 35 future planned constellations are considered. For non-constellation launches instead economic time series methods such as the Seasonal Auto Regressive Integrated Moving Average model and the Long Short-Term Memory model are employed. It is shown that the Seasonal Auto Regressive Integrated Moving Average model clearly outperforms the Long Short-Term Memory model. The increase in launch traffic does not happen in a vacuum and is greatly influenced by outside factors such as the general economy. As a novelty, this work also includes the global Gross Domestic Product as an economic influence on the satellite launch traffic. Including the Gross Domestic Product as an influence in the launch traffic improved predictions by 53%. Combining both constellations and non-constellation, the yearly number of objects launched could reach up to 12,000. This huge number demonstrates the need for guidelines for future launches and mitigation measures. • Satellite la

title: Scaling Sustainable Propellants to Address Rocket Emissions: Lessons From the U.S. Aviation Industry
summary: Examines scaling sustainable propellants to address rocket emissions, drawing lessons from US aviation.
abstract: The rapid growth of the U.S. commercial space industry has exposed a profound regulatory gap in addressing rocket emissions. By releasing greenhouse gases and particulates like black carbon, alumina, and water vapor, rocket launches not only contribute to climate change but also accelerate stratospheric ozone depletion. The U.S. aviation industry encountered similar environmental challenges decades ago, which eventually prompted legal and policy frameworks to curtail aviation emission through sustainable fuel technologies. Unlike aviation, however, the space industry now operates in a legal vacuum, with no binding international environmental standards or domestic regulations targeting rocket atmospheric pollution. As rocket emissions penetrate into every layer of the atmosphere, their environmental risks are even more intensified and distinct from aviation emissions. This Note argues that sustainable rocket technologies, such as green propellants and green non-chemical propulsion systems, offer an effective pathway to contain rocket emissions. Drawing lessons from the U.S. aviation industry’s gradual regulatory evolution, the Note proposes that a proactive regulatory framework, including industry-specific emission standards, incentive programs, and international collaboration, is critical for the U.S. space industry to avoid replicating aviation’s delayed response and to ensure that the new space era proceeds within environmentally sustainable bounds.

title: Small change or big bang? The shift from legacy to new space project planning
summary: Examines the shift from legacy to new space project planning in space organisations.
abstract: Traditionally, space organisations have considered space projects a means to deliver specific outputs against a predefined mission scope. This is the so-called “outcome-based perspective” of which “landing the first man on the Moon” is an exemplary case. However, this conceptualisation is outdated and inadequate in the context of the New Space Economy; the outcome-based perspective cannot describe the value that can be created and captured by commercial space projects. This requires a paradigm shift in planning new space projects, a topic that has so far received little attention among scholars and practitioners. To this end, we answer the question: “How does project planning differ between legacy and new space projects?”. Based on 40 interviews with managers developing legacy and new space projects, we provide a conceptual framework to understand the differences between planning legacy and new space projects, highlighting the key dimensions of scope, actors, measurement, time, governance and risk. We explain why it occurs, leveraging the modern and better-suited “value-based perspective”, rooted in the mainstream literature on complex project value and value theory. This research extends the body of knowledge on the planning and development of new commercial space projects toward space sustainability. It offers practical insights to managers in the industry and to officers in space agencies to develop new space projects that generate long-term economic, social and environmen

title: Solar Thermal Propulsion System for Lunar CubeSat Launch:A Lean Architecture Using Inflatable Concentrators and In-Situ Resource Utilization
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
summary: Presents a solar thermal propulsion system using ISRU to launch 50 kg satellites to lunar orbit with 97% mass reduction versus tether architectures.
abstract: This research presents a solar thermal propulsion system for launching 50 kg operational satellites to 100 km lunar orbit, achieving a 97% mass reduction compared to orbital tether architectures. The system deploys 2.5 tonnes of infrastructure comprising 50 inflatable parabolic reflectors (10 m diameter) that concentrate 1,361 W/m² lunar solar flux to generate 4.5 MW thermal power at a tungsten-rhenium heat exchanger operating at 2,200 K. The architecture produces 2,000 N continuous thrust, accelerating a 500 kg vehicle at 4 g—compatible with standard CubeSat components without high-g hardening. Specific impulse ranges from 190 seconds using lunar water-derived steam to 450 seconds with liquid hydrogen. A 50-meter electromagnetic launch rail provides initial vectoring, with burnout at 1.68 km/s achieving lunar orbital velocity after 4 minutes of powered flight. The system is designed for phased in-situ resource utilization, transitioning from imported propellant to hydrogen electrolyzed from confirmed Shackleton Crater water ice deposits. Unlike electromagnetic mass drivers requiring 400+ g acceleration or rotovator tethers demanding 85 tonnes of orbital infrastructure, this solar thermal approach leverages abundant lunar solar energy while preserving payload survivability for operational spacecraft missions including lunar relay networks and surface mapping constellations.

title: Space Diplomacy and International Collaboration
summary: Analyses space diplomacy and international collaboration amid shifting geopolitics among space stakeholders.
abstract: The space frontier has historically served as a nexus for scientific and technological collaboration. However, the geopolitical landscape surrounding space activities has undergone significant transformations in recent years, significantly impacting the major dynamics of relationships among space stakeholders. The chapter employs a rigorous analytical approach to examine the efficacy of space diplomacy in fostering international collaboration within the space domain. The study examines significant developments in space diplomacy since the Cold War, explores how emerging space actors, including states and non-states, are reshaping the dynamics of international space governance, and argues that space diplomacy will play a critical role in addressing global challenges in the international system. By providing a comprehensive analysis of space diplomacy efforts, the chapter offers insights into how science diplomacy can help manage competition and cooperation in the final frontier.

title: Space Economy Research Trends for Foresight Analysis
venue: Journal of Aerospace Technology and Management
summary: Space economy research trends for foresight analysis.
abstract: ABSTRACT A recent economic sector, the space economy, has been the subject of discussions at several international events, including the G20, COPUOS, and the World Economic Forum. The evolution of space activities from the traditional space era to the New Space era influences market shares in the global economy. This study aims to identify trends in space economics studies conducted up to 2023. The study used the Google Scholar database with space economy and valuation size of space economy as keywords. Further bibliometric analysis was conducted using VOSviewer, Publish or Perish, and then artificial intelligence (AI) (ChatGPT). The study aims to identify the current direction in space economy research in terms of its subjects, issues, innovation, and publishing output. In addition to global trend research, a study was carried out on the space economy in Indonesia. However, the amount of research on the space economy in Indonesia, however, is still very limited in terms of case studies, which restricts a comprehensive description of the Indonesian space sector and industry. The research also shows how the space economy, as a sector, contributes to creating income for the economy.

title: Space Economy and Sustainable Development Goals: Technological Spin-offs and Policies for Emerging Economies
venue: South India Journal of Social Sciences
summary: Qualitatively analyses the space economy as a driver of development via technological spin-offs and policy for emerging economies.
abstract: Space economy, worldwide, has been transformed from being a field of scientific discovery to being critical infrastructure to support sustainable development. The present qualitative study analyzes its role in being a driver for development through its various economic, sociological, technological and policy perspectives for developing countries. Based on the institutional perspective provided in UN and OECD documents, the article shows the utility of space services in achieving Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). The paper claims that lowering of launch costs and international collaborations have created new possibilities for the Global South. The article presents case studies from African and Latin American continents, and from India in terms of shifting to a demand driven approach in order to provide practical guidance to technological self-sufficiency. However, such a potential can be harnessed only through appropriate frameworks which match the economics and priorities of the country concerned. The paper ends with providing policy imperatives for emerging economies based on such an institutional framework.

summary: Review of a book on space law and management of outer space resources.
abstract: "Space Law and the Management of Outer Space Resources," authored by Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, and published in 2013 in New York, USA, offers a comprehensive exploration of the legal frameworks governing the utilization of extraterrestrial resources. As humanity's ventures into space intensify, the need for clear legal guidelines becomes paramount. This book delves into the intricacies of space law, addressing the challenges and opportunities associated with managing resources beyond our planet. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, recognized the accelerating pace of space exploration and the pressing need for robust legal structures to oversee the extraction and use of outer space resources. With private enterprises and nations alike setting their sights on celestial bodies, the potential for both collaboration and conflict has grown. This book, published in New York in 2013, aims to shed light on the existing legal frameworks and propose pathways for harmonious and equitable resource management in space. Central to this work are the foundational treaties and principles that constitute space law. The Outer Space Treaty of 1967 serves as the cornerstone, establishing that outer space is free for exploration and use by all countries and is not subject to national appropriation by any means. Building upon this, Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad elucidates concepts such as the non-appropriation principle, the common heritage of mankind, and the freedom o

title: Space Sustainability - Sustainability, ESG and CSR in the Space Industry
summary: Dissertation on sustainability, ESG and CSR in the space industry.
abstract: The rapid expansion of the space industry has intensified the need to examine sustainability, Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR), and Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) practices in a sector traditionally driven by technological advancement, strategic competition, and public investment. This thesis investigates how businesses in the space sector define and report on sustainability and assesses the degree to which their reporting practices demonstrate significant commitments to space sustainability. The study assesses both public and private actors and explores whether reporting approaches differ according to organizational type, regional context, and position in the space value chain. The research adopts qualitative multiple-case study design supported by abductive reasoning and qualitative content analysis. Nine case studies were selected to represent a broad range of actors, including European private firms, European aerospace primes, United States commercial companies, and public agencies. The empirical material consists of annual reports, CSR reports, ESG reports, and sustainability reports. To structure the analysis, a dedicated Data Collection Matrix was developed in Excel, enabling systematic coding of sustainability-related content. The analysis was carried out on two interconnected levels: first, through SDG linked coding based on the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, and second, through a space-specific sustainability matrix capturing themes

title: Space Sustainability: The Global Commons
summary: Preprint on space sustainability as a global commons as space becomes critical infrastructure and commercial zone.
abstract: Space is no longer a distant, barely reachable frontier of scientific exploration; it has become a critical infrastructure for life on Earth and a rapidly expanding zone of intense commercial activity. Yet this expansion is unfolding in ways that replicate, and amplify, the unsustainable dynamics already driving ecological and social crises on our planet. This chapter explains the concept of space sustainability as a multidimensional challenge; it raises the questions of governance, knowledge, power, justice, and global responsibility. It highlights both the profound benefits derived from space activities and the uneven distribution of costs and risks, from orbital debris and atmospheric impacts to privatization of essential services. We therefore argue that it frames space as a global commons that demands stewardship rather than pure exploitation, cooperation rather than competition, and governance that prioritizes long-term wellbeing rather than laissez-faire approach. Sustainability in space is inseparable from sustainability on Earth. This chapter invites readers, whether they are space administration and industry actors, policymakers, scientists, or simply engaged citizens, to see space not as a limitless frontier, but as a shared domain whose future depends on collective choices made today.

title: Space debris and outer space sustainability: legal challenges
summary: Examines legal challenges of space debris and sustainability as orbit is seen as finite.
abstract: By 2025, humankind had reached a turning point in space. The orbital environment, once considered effectively unlimited, is now increasingly understood as a finite and congested operational domain. This article presents an in-depth evaluation of the legal and policy regimes for space sustainability, along with a comparison with the physical challenges posed by space debris, which continue to grow while the treaty regime in place was drafted in the context of the Cold War era. This paper draws upon the European Space Agency Annual Space Environment Report 2025 and extensive amount of legal research to conclude that the present framework is structurally not well suited to combat the generation of cascading debris, which is a feature of the Kessler Syndrome, through voluntary soft-law guidelines and fault-based liability standards. The discussion identifies a growing governance gap in which the rapid deployment of mega-constellations and the rise of Active Debris Removal (ADR) technologies are far exceeding the development of binding international law. Furthermore, this report highlights a discontinuity in the global legal order by presenting the regulatory differences between the EU law-driven market proposal of the EU Space Act and the US-based coordination-driven regulatory approach. The current study does not offer completely new models for reform, but rather takes stock of the ongoing discourse regarding the need for a more stringent Space Traffic Management (STM) regime, c

title: Space debris material sourcing for in-space manufacturing: a quantitative evaluation framework
summary: Proposes a quantitative framework for evaluating space debris as material feedstock for in-space manufacturing.
abstract: The increasing accumulation of space debris presents significant challenges to sustainable space exploration while offering opportunities for material reuse through in-space manufacturing. This research presents a framework for deriving the comprehensive value associated with using the growing space debris population as a material sourcing option for future in-space manufacturing. The growth rate of the space debris population in low Earth orbit is derived using a material flow analysis for future launch rate estimates up to the year 2050. Using these estimates, a total value calculation for space debris material sourcing is determined by considering the value associated with space debris’s material market value, transportation cost reduction, and object removal risk reduction. The results of this framework indicate that cost savings from reduced material transportation to space are the most significant driver for overall space debris value, significantly outweighing the contributions of material and risk reduction value. As more data become available regarding in-space manufacturing capabilities, this framework provides insights regarding the composition of space debris value and assesses the economic viability of space debris reuse.

title: Space economy and strategic development in ASEAN pathways to 2035
summary: Projects the ASEAN space economy reaching USD 80-200 billion by 2035, driven by Earth observation, satellite communications and defence ISR demand.
abstract: The ASEAN space economy is entering a rapid growth phase toward 2035, alongside a global market projected to reach USD 1.8 trillion. ASEAN’s share is expected to scale to approximately USD 80–200 billion, driven by three key engines: Earth Observation (EO) commercialization, SATCOM expansion via high-throughput systems, and rising demand for ISR and Space Domain Awareness (SDA). EO in Southeast Asia alone is projected to triple to USD 45 billion by 2030. Thailand is positioned as a regional hub through THEOS-2, Thaicom platforms, national space policy, and a multi-orbit spaceport strategy enabling upstream and downstream integration. Using a bottom-up forecast model aligned with the Space Capacity Ladder (SCL), ASEAN is expected to sustain a 4.4–11.1% share of the global space economy by 2035, led by Thailand, Indonesia, Vietnam, Malaysia, Singapore, and the Philippines.

abstract: The development of space-based solar energy (SBSP) in the last decade goes beyond scientific and technical experiments and acquires the features of an emerging sector of the global economy. In contrast to the works focused on technological aspects or the environmental agenda, the study considers SBSP as an area of intersection of long-term investment strategies, national priorities of energy security and new market opportunities. The subject of the analysis is the country models of SBSP development, their institutional design and economic parameters determining the prospects for the orbital stations’ commercialization. The purpose of the work is to identify the dominant national strategies in the sphere of space energy and to determine the threshold values of indicators ensuring its economic feasibility. The relevance of the topic is due to the intensification of programs in the United States, China, Japan, India, Russia and the European Union, which consider SBSP as a tool for reducing dependence on traditional energy carriers and consolidating technological leadership. The methodological framework includes comparative country analysis, modeling with the decomposition of factor influences on LCOE, as well as analysis of strategic documents and reporting data. SpaceX, the East India Company, and the political economy of space
summary: Argues state and corporate vehicles project national power into space, comparing SpaceX to the East India Company.
abstract: Private corporations and state-owned enterprises are becoming increasingly important vehicles through which nations project power into space. This paper argues that the emerging political economy of space displays institutional dynamics reminiscent of an earlier era of frontier expansion: the Age of Sail dominated by the European East India Companies. Drawing on original data on the concentration of global launch capacity and on the historical record of chartered-company governance, we show how frontier firms can accumulate concentrated market power, exploit legal ambiguity, blur the boundary between public and private authority, and gradually acquire governance-like functions in domains beyond effective sovereign reach. Using Susan Strange’s framework of structural power, we explain why geopolitical competition generates incentives for regulatory forbearance, as states become increasingly dependent on their national champions. The historical record suggests that once dependence on a dominant provider becomes entrenched, governance reform tends to occur only after crises, coming at high costs. We conclude by outlining policy implications for the governance of the emerging space economy.

title: Spacepower in the Second Space Age
summary: Book on how commercialisation and democratisation of space shape spacepower.
abstract: This book investigates how the processes of commercialisation and democratisation of space have impacted the development of spacepower within the context of the “Second Space Age”. The main characteristic of the “Second Space Age” is the relative detachment of the bulk of human space activities from the goals and aims of governments. In essence, it means that we live in a time when commercial activities shape, to a great extent, the patterns of utilisation of outer space. This book recognises spacepower not only as a tool wielded by a nation-state for its own purposes but also as an attribute of the whole nation, not necessarily under the direct control of the state authority. The volume presents a theoretical model of spacepower that defines the terms structural spacepower, national spacepower and commercial spacepower to characterise the nature of spacepower in the Second Space Age. Subsequently, it also outlines procedures for measuring and comparing the spacepower of individual actors and nations. This book will be of interest to students of space power, strategic studies, air power, and International Relations.

summary: Argues Starship enables faster, more ambitious missions to Europa by easing propulsive energy constraints.
abstract: Abstract Europa’s astrobiological promise is matched by the severity of its engineering constraints. The propulsive energy required to reach the surface of Europa diminishes potential science payloads to the point at which historical flagship mission plans, using expendable rockets like the SLS, would deliver less than 50kg to Europa, with a transit time of over 6 years. In this paper, we show the feasibility of the SpaceX Starship delivering payloads of 10000kg or more, directly to the surface of Europa, with transit times of less than 2.5 years.

title: Suing Foreign States after Devas Ltd. v. Antrix Corp. Ltd.
summary: Analyses US jurisdiction over foreign states after Devas v. Antrix, arising from a satellite-related arbitration agreement.
abstract: As the number of public and private space-based activities increases, jurisdictional questions and choice of law also present new options for litigants. In CC/Devas (Mauritius) Ltd. v. Antrix Corp. Ltd., decided in 2025, the United States Supreme Court determined that a federal court could address claims related to an arbitration agreement between a private Indian telecommunications company as plaintiff and a corporation of the State of India as defendant. The Court held that the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act of 1976, which would ordinarily immunise a foreign State defendant from liability in the United States, did not apply in this case based on its enumerated exceptions. The decision specifically addressed a geostationary satellite service contract. This article identifies several factors that may attract or deter plaintiffs considering filing a claim against a foreign State in a foreign legal system in matters regarding commercial space activities and arbitral award enforcement, with potential indirect effects on the development of other areas of space law.

title: Supply chain due diligence in space-based manufacturing and lunar resource extraction: building sustainable & resilient cislunar operations
summary: Examines supply chain due diligence for space-based manufacturing and lunar resource extraction.
abstract: Abstract Space is moving from episodic missions to continuous industrial activity. Space-based manufacturing in microgravity and the extraction of lunar resources through in-situ resource utilisation are now anchored in engineering roadmaps and national regulations, not only in scientific aspiration. Reviews of in-space manufacturing show a steady shift toward orbital assembly lines, additive manufacturing, and on-orbit servicing as enabling infrastructure for a growing commercial space economy. In parallel, technical literature on lunar ISRU highlights water-ice excavation, oxygen production from regolith, and additive construction as prerequisites for extended lunar presence and for cheaper in-space logistics. These developments create a cislunar supply chain that loops between Earth, orbit, lunar orbit, and the lunar surface. The chain is long, capital-intensive, highly autonomous, and legally hybrid, because private operators act under state authorisation and continuing supervision under the Outer Space Treaty. At the same time, terrestrial regulation is hardening supply chain due diligence into binding law. The EU Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive requires large firms to identify, prevent, mitigate and remedy human rights and environmental harms across their chain of activities, with monitoring and liability for failure. This paper is a doctrinal and conceptual study that brings these two trajectories together. It maps the cislunar supply chain, explains w

title: Sustainable Space Operations: Navigating Emerging Technologies, Debris Management, and Governance Challenges for the Future.
venue: BCU Open Access Repository (Birmingham City University)
summary: Dissertation on sustainability of orbital space: debris management, emerging technologies and governance challenges.
abstract: The sustainability of Earth’s orbital environment has emerged as one of the defining challenges of 21st-century space activity. As space becomes increasingly commercialised, privatised, and accessible, our space orbits, once perceived as vast and inexhaustible, are showing signs of critical stress. This thesis investigates the multifaceted dynamics shaping sustainable orbital operations, examining the projected risks of orbital overcrowding, the future of space tourism, and the role of patent-driven technological innovation in addressing space debris. Together, these dimensions form an integrated framework for understanding how humanity can navigate the tensions between innovation, exploitation, and preservation in outer space. This thesis is structured as three independent but related papers that explore the sustainability challenges of space, defined in this thesis as Earth’s orbital environment rather than the practically infinite expanse of deep space. The sustainability challenges of space are explored, through the lens of emerging technologies, debris management, and governance challenges, this research aims to inform readers on the complexities and opportunities for sustainable space development. The first paper (chapter 2) focuses on the issue of orbital crowding and debris, presenting Earth’s orbit as a finite, congested resource and a textbook example of an Area Beyond National Jurisdiction (ABNJ). A version of this paper was published as (Martin-Lawson et al., 2024

title: Sustainable Water Systems in Space: A Review of Current Technologies and Future Prospects
summary: Reviews current technologies and prospects for sustainable water systems in space.
abstract: Abstract Sustainable water management is a critical challenge in space exploration, where the limited availability of resources requires innovative approaches to ensure astronauts' survival on long‐duration missions. This narrative review explores the key technologies and methods involved in water recycling, in situ resource utilization (ISRU), and bioregenerative life support systems (BLSS) essential for supporting human life in space. The Environmental Control and Life Support System (ECLSS) aboard the International Space Station has demonstrated significant progress in recycling water from urine, sweat, and humidity, achieving up to 93% recovery. However, challenges remain in reducing energy consumption, improving system durability, and ensuring water quality. ISRU technologies, particularly those aimed at extracting water ice from lunar and Martian environments, offer promising solutions for future missions, but they must overcome scalability and logistical hurdles. This review also highlights the potential of nanotechnology and AI‐driven autonomous systems in enhancing water purification and management. Nanomaterials like graphene oxide membranes could revolutionize filtration efficiency, while AI could optimize real‐time water quality monitoring and recycling processes. As space agencies push toward establishing colonies on the Moon and Mars, the development of sustainable, closed‐loop water systems will be pivotal to the success of these missions. title: The Artemis Accords and the Evolution of Space Law: Navigating Customary Norms, Resource Exploitation, and Sovereign Ambitions
summary: Analyses how the Artemis Accords shift international space law on customary norms, resource exploitation and sovereignty.
abstract: The Artemis Accords, established on 13 October 2020, mark a decisive methodological shift in international space governance. Rather than seeking a formal multilateral treaty through the United Nations Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space (COPUOS), the United States has pursued a strategy of recruiting signatory nations into bilateral commitments that operationalise a contested interpretation of the Outer Space Treaty of 1967. With 67 signatories as of May 2026, the Accords command significant multilateral support. Yet they have achieved this at the cost of legal fragmentation and a deepening challenge to the foundational principle of Article I of the OST, which declares outer space the province of all mankind. This paper examines three interlocking legal disputes that the Accords have brought to the surface. First, it analyses the tension between Article II of the OST, which prohibits national appropriation of outer space, and Section 10(2) of the Accords, which asserts that the commercial extraction of space resources does not constitute such appropriation. Second, it examines the legality of safety zones introduced under Section 11(1) of the Accords and the structural risk that these zones function as instruments of de facto territorial exclusion without triggering the express prohibitions of Article II. Third, it addresses the geopolitical consequences of the bifurcation between the Artemis bloc and the Sino-Russian International Lunar Research Station framework,

title: The Circular Space Economy: Review, Conceptualization, and Research Agenda for Narrowing, Slowing, and Closing the Loop in Orbit
summary: Reviews the circular space economy and sets a research agenda for narrowing, slowing and closing loops.
abstract: The Space Economy (SE) is rapidly expanding, yet its reliance on a linear production and consumption model is intensifying the orbital debris problem and stands in tension with the core principles of a Circular Economy (CE). Despite increasing attention to both domains, scholarship at their intersection remains fragmented and conceptually underdeveloped, limiting cumulative theorizing on how circularity can be conceptualized in SE contexts. Addressing this gap, I conduct an integrative review of CE and SE research published between 2010 and 2025, synthesizing the contemporary literature into an organizing framework for conceptualizing the Circular Space Economy (CSE). Building on this synthesis, I advance a ten-point research agenda structured across four distinct yet interdependent pillars: (1) Orbital Property Rights and Governance; (2) Circular Ecosystems and Supply Chains; (3) Circular Business Models and Circular Product Design & Technologies; and (4) Methods and Metrics for CSE. This agenda supports future theory development and empirical research and offers a roadmap for scholars, policymakers, and industry leaders to secure the orbital environment and advance circular resource stewardship on Earth.

title: The Completed Abundance Economy Part V Orbital AI Data Centers Powered by Dyson Swarms (2026–2040): Feasibility & Impact
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

abstract: The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence is driving sharp increases in data-center energy consumption, water use, and land demand, affecting terrestrial infrastructure and environments. In this paper, I examine orbital AI data centers powered by Dyson swarm–like solar satellite constellations. These systems would place large-scale AI compute platforms in Earth orbit, supplying them with locally harvested solar energy instead of terrestrial grids. Operating in space offers continuous high-intensity solar power and passive radiative cooling in vacuum, eliminating water-intensive cooling, cutting carbon emissions, and freeing AI growth from Earth’s environmental limits. I assess technical feasibility through modular satellite architectures, solar power generation and storage, radiative thermal management, high-bandwidth optical communications, orbital mechanics, and launch logistics enabled by reusable heavy-lift vehicles such as Starship. I compare orbital and terrestrial data centers in terms of energy efficiency, water consumption, land use, life-cycle emissions, and long-term cost per unit of computation. I also address strategic and geopolitical issues, including spectrum allocation, orbital congestion and debris risks, regulatory challenges from recent FCC filings, and potential concentration of orbital compute capacity. Finally, I explore business models and impacts on cloud services, AI training economics, and competition among technology and aerospace leaders. I c

venue: International journal of high school research

abstract: As demand for rare Earth minerals rises, access to these resources has become a growing concern.One promising solution is asteroid mining.Near-Earth asteroids are known to contain quantities of valuable materials such as nickel, cobalt, platinum group metals, water, and ice.These resources are essential for advanced manufacturing, energy systems, and space refueling.This paper surveys the feasibility of space-based mining, outlining the technical, logistical, and economic challenges involved.We discuss the process of asteroid selection, progress in on-board and Autonomous robot systems, and in-space resource processing.Recent works suggest that asteroid mining could become viable within the next two decades.If successfully implemented, asteroid mining can significantly change geo-political resource contention and reduce the scarcity of many important elements.

abstract: This paper analyzes the rapid growth of the small satellite market and the resulting structural shifts in global space transportation.Between 2025 and 2034, approximately 43,193 satellites are projected for launch, with mega-constellations accounting for 66% of demand, concentrated predominantly in LEO.The global space transportation market is expected to reach $175 billion over this period, driven largely by mega-constellation deployment and rising defense demand.SpaceX's dominance in reusable launch technology is reshaping the competitive landscape, prompting rivals to pursue vehicle upscaling, reusability, and automation.Meanwhile, growing demand for VLEO and EHR observation, alongside the emergence of OTV and space logistics services, is extending the scope of space transportation beyond conventional launch to inter-orbit delivery.Major spacefaring nations are strengthening PPP to secure strategic launch autonomy and address defense requirements.This paper examines these global trends and presents policy implications for South Korea's space transportation sector.초 록 본 논문은 소형 위성 시장의 급성장과 이에 따른 글로벌 우주수송 분야의 구조적 변화를 분석한다.2025~2034년 약 43,193기의 위성 발사가 전망되며, Mega-constellations이 전체의 66%를 차지하고 LEO 궤 도에 집중될 것으로 예상된다

The Legal Philosophy of Space Civilization
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
summary: Title only: book-length treatment of the legal philosophy of governing a space civilization.
abstract: Humanity has learned how to leave Earth. It has not yet learned how to govern the universe. The Legal Philosophy of Space Civilization is a groundbreaking exploration of one of the greatest unanswered questions in legal and political philosophy: Can law exist where no sovereign may ever rule? Drawing upon the Outer Space Treaty, classical jurisprudence, and contemporary debates on commercial space exploration, Northon Salomão de Oliveira challenges the territorial assumptions that have defined legal systems for thousands of years. Through an original synthesis of legal theory, philosophy, history, and international law, the book introduces the provocative concept of "orphan jurisdiction": a legal order deliberately created without territorial sovereignty, existing beyond the traditional foundations of political authority. Engaging with the ideas of Hans Kelsen, H. L. A. Hart, Ronald Dworkin, Lon Fuller, David Hume, and modern space law, the author examines property rights over asteroids, Martian citizenship, interplanetary liability, the limits of constitutional governance across astronomical distances, and the emerging legal architecture of humanity's expansion beyond Earth. More than a study of space law, this work is a profound meditation on the future of justice itself. As civilization prepares to establish permanent settlements on the Moon and Mars, it asks whether the oldest assumptions of jurisprudence can survive a world where territory no longer defines authority. title: The Lunar Stairway: An Orbital-Platform-First Paradigm for Lunar Development and Its Engineering Rationale
summary: Argues an orbital-platform-first paradigm for lunar development against surface-first bases, with engineering rationale.
abstract: Abstract Objective: To examine the mainstream premise that lunar development must be based on the lunar surface; to argue the engineering rationale for building long-term residential bases, production facilities, and logistics hubs first in circumlunar orbit rather than on the lunar surface; and to propose a system design for the “Lunar Stairway” (a distributed system of circumlunar platform ports). Methods: On the basis of orbital mechanics (the vis-viva equation and the rocket equation), the velocity increments and mass penalties of lunar-surface landing and departure were calculated and compared with those of residence in circumlunar orbit; the success rate of lunar soft-landing missions worldwide from 1966 to 2025 was tallied; scientific assessments of the Apollo moonquake network, the Chang’e-4 in situ radiation measurements on the lunar surface, and the health effects of lunar dust were compiled; and a ballistic delivery and interception–deceleration model for the “circumlunar platform–capsule projectile–cable-net/pit/sponge-lake splashdown” system was established. Results: A one-way landing on the lunar surface requires a velocity increment of approximately 1.9 km/s (with I sp = 300 s, propellant accounts for approximately 47.6% of the initial mass), and departure from the Moon requires a further approximately 1.85 km/s. title: The Lunar Water Rush: Space Resource Rights, Safety Zones, and India's Regulatory Concern
venue: International Journal of Law Management & Humanities
summary: Analyses lunar water resource rights, safety zones and India's regulatory concerns.
abstract: The Moon is becoming a realistic site for scientific missions, permanent research facilities, and commercial activity. One resource has become especially important: water ice near the lunar south pole. Lunar water is extremely valuable for future commercial space operations. Yet international space law does not clearly answer who may extract it, own it after extraction, exclude others from a working area, or resolve conflicts between competing missions. This paper examines the legal gap between the non-appropriation rule in Article II of the Outer Space Treaty 1967 and the growing practice of commercial space-resource extraction. It argues that the most difficult issue is not simply whether a company can own extracted lunar water. The harder issue is whether “safety zones” around lunar operations may become de facto exclusive areas, allowing powerful States and companies to control the most useful sites without formally claiming sovereignty. The Artemis Accords support resource extraction and coordination zones, while the United Nations Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space is developing non-binding principles on space-resource activities. India’s Space Policy 2023 also allows non-government entities to commercially recover, possess, own, transport, use, and sell space resources. The paper argues that India should create a transparent national licensing framework before Indian private entities undertake lunar-resource activities. The framework should require mission a

title: The Martian Gold Frontier: Geochemical Potential, Extraction Technologies, and Techno-Economic Pathways for Precious-Metal Mining in the Inner Solar System
summary: Assesses geochemical potential, extraction technologies and techno-economic pathways for Martian gold as supply moves beyond terrestrial launch.
abstract: Human expansion beyond Earth requires a transition from supply architectures dominated by terrestrial launch to systems capable of identifying, extracting, and transforming extraterrestrial resources. This article critically evaluates the potential for gold (Au), platinum-group elements (PGEs), and strategic metals on Mars, placing the Red Planet at the center of a possible inner-Solar-System mineral economy. An integrative review of 40 scientific sources with verifiable DOIs covers Martian geochemistry, meteorites, highly siderophile elements, magmatic and hydrothermal metallogenesis, impacts, water and ice, in-situ resource utilization (ISRU), drilling, regolith processing, asteroids, the Martian moons, and space economics. Evidence confirms Au and other HSEs in Martian materials, while plausible concentration mechanisms include sulfide segregation, hydrothermal activity, impact systems, and sedimentary processes. No direct evidence, however, demonstrates a Martian gold deposit with grade, tonnage, and continuity sufficient for classification as an exploitable resource. A Space Gold Prospectivity Index (SGPI) is proposed to prioritize exploration targets by integrating geology, accessibility, water, energy, technology maturity, and uncertainty. title: The Mission Market: Flying NASA's Vetted, Unflown Science
summary: Proposes a mission market to fly NASA-validated science missions that the agency cannot afford.
abstract: Every year NASA validates more excellent science missions than it can afford to fly. Some of the most promising missions in astrophysics, heliophysics, and planetary science are judged selectable, yet remain grounded indefinitely. Mission Market is an advance market commitment that can fly lower cost missions without competing for federal appropriations. Funding comes primarily from the enormous capital now flowing into artificial intelligence (AI) companies that value generating frontier data for scientific foundation models and is also supplemented by traditional means such as philanthropy and patron-scientists.

The Need for Cislunar Governance: Environmental Security and Sustainability Challenges
venue: International Journal for the Semiotics of Law - Revue internationale de Sémiotique juridique
summary: Argues for cislunar governance as the region becomes an arena of geopolitical competition with environmental security challenges.
abstract: Abstract The cislunar space, i.e., that region beyond geostationary orbit and the Moon, is rapidly shifting from a scientific, space exploration outpost to an arena of competing geopolitical interests, commercial expansion, and resource exploitation. As countries and private companies alike plans missions to the Moon, the sustainability problems plaguing near-Earth space threaten to follow them along, raising critical questions of environmental security in a domain where physical conditions are different, legal frameworks inexistent, and governance structures still to be developed. Through a gap analysis methodology that identifies key environmental challenges, this study argues that an effective cislunar governance is a precondition for addressing them and offers some recommendations to address the most urgent ones on our way to the Moon.

title: The Obligation to Conduct Environmental Impact Assessments in the Sustainable Development of Mega-Constellations
summary: Examines the obligation to conduct environmental impact assessments for sustainable development of satellite mega-constellations.
abstract: Abstract The development of satellite mega-constellations promises substantial benefits but also exacerbates environmental risks, including primarily the proliferation of space debris, interference with astronomy, and effects on the atmosphere. This article explains the critical role of environmental impact assessments (EIAs) in ensuring the sustainable development of mega-constellations and argues that EIAs should be regarded as part of existing international space law. On the one hand, heightened environmental risks from space activities render EIAs increasingly relevant, if not indispensable, for implementing the obligations under Article IX of the Outer Space Treaty. On the other hand, while Article III of the Treaty enables the application of general international law on EIAs to outer space, its scope is constrained to activities that are likely to cause a significant adverse impact. The analysis also addresses the operationalization of EIAs with regard to mega-constellations by identifying the responsible state, assessing the significance of environmental impacts, articulating minimum standards, and developing appropriate mechanisms.

The Rational Design of Space Agreements: How Bilateralism Shapes Powerful States' Design Preferences
summary: Introduces a dataset of 952 space agreements to analyse how bilateralism shapes powerful states' institutional design preferences in space governance.
abstract: ABSTRACT The global governance of outer space relies heavily on international agreements, yet the institutional forms of these agreements remain underexplored. This article introduces a new dataset on various design features of 952 space agreements, offering the first large‐N overview of institutional design in space governance. Building on rational design theory, this article analyzes how these design features interact with one another and with negotiation structures. Our results reveal systematic trade‐offs and suggest that power asymmetry has contrasting effects depending on the context: Powerful states tend to favor greater delegation, precision, and enforcement in bilateral agreements, while often resisting them in multilateral settings. These findings underscore the importance of accounting for both power dynamics and bilateralism, two contextual factors often overlooked in rational design theory. By making the dataset publicly available, the article seeks to foster further research on the causes and consequences of institutional variation in space governance and to advance comparative institutionalist scholarship across issue‐areas of global governance.

title: The Regulation of Commercial Space Tourism Under International Space Law: Challenges, Gaps, and the Need for a Comprehensive International Legal Framework
summary: Examines regulation of commercial space tourism, its gaps and the need for a comprehensive international framework.
abstract: Commercial space tourism has evolved from a futuristic concept into an emerging global industry driven by private aerospace companies such as Blue Origin, Virgin Galactic, and SpaceX. Successful suborbital flights have demonstrated that commercial human spaceflight is no longer limited to government astronauts but is increasingly accessible to paying private individuals, creating significant opportunities for technological innovation, economic growth, and international cooperation. This transition, however, has also exposed deficiencies in the international legal framework governing outer space. The five principal United Nations space treaties were negotiated between 1967 and 1979, at a time when states were the exclusive actors in space exploration, and they contain little guidance on private commercial spaceflight, passenger status, insurance, or environmental protection. This article examines the adequacy of that framework in regulating commercial space tourism, evaluating the legal status of spaceflight participants, the allocation of liability among states and private operators, passenger safety standards, insurance requirements, environmental sustainability, and consumer protection. Through comparative analysis of national regulatory approaches in the United States, the United Kingdom, the United Arab Emirates, Japan, and Nigeria, the article demonstrates that domestic law alone cannot effectively govern an inherently transnational industry, and that the resulting fragm

abstract: The U.S. space industry accounts for more than half of the global space economy, reflecting its significant economic influence. It has been realized that quantitative data have been used as the existing literature to analyse the spaceindustry’s economic impact. This study, which is based on qualitative data, aims to reflect in-depth expert knowledge and analysing through topic modelling. The main purpose of this study is examining NASA’s role, the involvement of other US government institutions, the growing presence of private enterprises and the public benefits gained through space expenditures in the US. This study examines all contributing factors within the space economy that impact the broader economy. This research is based on the qualitative data collected through semi-structured interviews along with broad contextual information. A total of 17 professionals from academia, government, and private industry in the United States shared their knowledge. Key themes emerged such as the relationship between the space industry and economic structures, economic benefits and growth, the role of the U.S. government in space economics, and the future of thespace economy. The analysis of the qualitative data through topic modelling indicates that the U.S. government’s strategic shifts and the rise of commercial space enterprises have reinforced economic interconnections within the industry, positioning it as a driver of innovation and growth. Moreover, the study addresses the econo

title: The Wicked Problem of Space Debris: From a Static Economic Lens to a System Dynamics View
summary: Applies a system dynamics view to the space debris problem against a static economic lens.
abstract: The global space economy, valued at approximately USD 400–630 billion (depending on definitional scope), is projected to expand rapidly, crossing USD 1 trillion as early as 2032 and reaching up to about USD 1.8 trillion by 2035. This growth has been driven by a surge (a roughly twelvefold increase) in satellite launches over the past decade, transforming Earth’s orbits into an increasingly congested domain plagued by space debris. The proliferation of space junk poses an escalating threat to orbital sustainability, yet effective governance mechanisms remain limited. This paper examines why conventional solutions for managing common-pool resources (command-and-control regulation, Pigouvian taxes, private property rights, allocation of tradable permits, and horizontal governance regimes) are not fully effective or are difficult to implement in addressing the orbital debris problem. Using a system dynamics perspective, the study qualitatively maps hypothesized feedback mechanisms shaping orbital expansion and space debris accumulation. It suggests that, under the assumed causal structure, reinforcing growth loops associated with geopolitical rivalry and commercial cost reductions linked to the New Space paradigm currently dominate over delayed balancing effects arising from the finite nature of orbital space, whose regenerative capacity is progressively degraded. There exists a threshold of exploitation beyond which orbital space effectively behaves as a non-renewable resource.

title: The circumstances of justice for the new space age: Distributive justice, scarcity and global governance
summary: Applies distributive justice, scarcity and global governance to the new space age.
abstract: Justice is fundamental to the Earth System Governance (ESG) literature, yet its application remains largely terrestrial. While scholarship has begun expanding ESG's scope to outer space, this paper identifies two critical challenges that impede this transition: the myth of resource abundance and unilateral governance regimes. To resolve the first obstacle, I introduce a definition of “New Space,” conceptualized through its contemporary ecosystem of diverse actors, activities, purposes, and places. I demonstrate how this lens debunks the myth of abundance by revealing that localized scarcity is an inherent feature of outer space resources, thereby activating the circumstances of justice. I then address the second obstacle by arguing that unilateral national legislation and first-possession legal proposals are structurally incompatible with distributive fairness, as they fail to establish an impartial architecture capable of resolving trans-jurisdictional conflict. By neutralizing these two barriers, this paper establishes a prolegomenon for any future theory of distributive justice for outer space governance.

title: The economics of outer space: Regulation, market failures, and industry prospects
summary: Space Policy survey by the Málaga and Bordeaux economists on regulation, market failures and industry prospects.
abstract: The past decade has witnessed a rapid expansion of human activity in Earth's orbit, elevating outer space as a domain of growing scientific, economic, and strategic importance. Yet this emerging sector is beset by market failures and regulatory gaps that hinder its growth and long-term viability: ill-defined property rights over extraterrestrial resources, orbital congestion, debris pollution, and the latent risk of weaponing commercial assets. The continued emergence of novel commercial applications is poised to amplify congestion and pollution frictions, bringing environmental concerns to the forefront of space policy analysis. This paper surveys foundational literature on the economics of outer space, highlighting connections to established areas of environmental, resource, and public economics. We argue that timely intervention is essential to unlock the sector’s economic potential and to mitigate conflict among spacefaring actors, and we identify open questions to guide future research in this promising and largely unexplored field.

title: The equity in outer space governance: A rethink of the role of developing nations in international space law
venue: International Journal of Law Justice and Jurisprudence
summary: Rethinks the role of developing nations in equity and international space law governance.
abstract: The governance of outer space is anchored in the principles of peaceful use, non-appropriation, and the "province of all mankind," as codified in the 1967 Outer Space Treaty (OST).The rapid commercialization of space activities and the dominance of technologically advanced states have exposed significant inequities within the current international legal regime.This article examines the concept of equity in outer space governance, explicitly reconceptualizing the role of developing nations in the formulation and application of international space law.Utilizing doctrinal legal analysis, the study argues that while the OST establishes formal legal equality, structural disparities in technological capacity, orbital access, and norm-setting authority undermine substantive equity.Furthermore, the article critiques emerging unilateral and bilateral frameworks, such as national space resource legislation and the Artemis Accords, for their potential to erode multilateralism and inclusivity.The study contends that international cooperation must be operationalized not merely as an aspiration, but as a mechanism for capacity building and technology transfer.It concludes that achieving true equity requires a shift from aspirational principles to practical, establish International Outer Space Authority, binding legal and institutional tools that guarantee the substantive participation of developing nations in preserving outer space as an intergenerational resource.

title: The military value of the Moon
The perils of periodising astropolitics: Space security and the system builders
summary: Argues against periodising astropolitics and discusses space security system builders.
abstract: Abstract Space systems are becoming an ever more important part of international security capabilities and practices. However, problematic interpretations of the Space Age are taking root in practitioner and academic circles along the contours of three sequential Space Ages. This article develops an original critique of these periodisations by applying a large technical systems approach and empirical research. It emphasises the role of space system builders and the prevalence of paradoxes in analysing space infrastructure as a method for critiquing three claims over the sweeping waves of democratisation, commercialisation, and militarisation in outer space that the periodisations make. This article proposes an alternative periodisation of a singular Global Space Age from 1957 that advances the counter-arguments that: first, power remains concentrated to a handful of space system builders rather than democratised to the many; second, that the space economy still relies on the state rather than being transferred to the private sector; and third, that the claims of sanctuary in space today ignore the spectre of space warfare that has long stalked space infrastructure. The infrastructural Global Space Age framing is offered as a useful materialist foundation for building bridges between international security, infrastructural technologies, and space security scholarship.

title: The science from asteroid sample return missions
The second space race and the astropolitical aspects of sino-american competition
summary: Analyses the Sino-American second space race and astropolitical competition.
abstract: Starting from the assumption that the United States and the People's Republic of China are engaged in competition for space primacy through the establishment of a permanent and dominant presence on the Moon, with the possibility of future exploitation of space resources, this paper aims to examine and explain the competition in question in its basic outlines. The analysis primarily focuses on the opposing Artemis and ILRS coalitions from both geopolitical and astropolitical perspectives. To that end, and within a realpolitik framework, the paper employs the methods of comparative analysis of the ongoing space activities of the two superpowers, their strategic documents and legislation, as well as the narratives of key actors. The research findings indicate that the world is currently witnessing the Second Space Race, which gives astropolitics increasing importance for understanding contemporary international relations. The conclusion emphasizes that, owing to new technological capabilities and emerging strategic circumstances, outer space is no longer primarily an area of scientific interest, but is increasingly manifesting itself as a distinct strategic domain of interstate competition. This entails numerous security, environmental, economic and other threats, but also opportunities for development.

title: The space economy is booming. Here's where most of the money is going
The value of lunar-derived oxygen and water for an early habitation customer
summary: Assesses the value of lunar-derived oxygen and water to an early lunar habitation customer needing life support consumables.
abstract: Establishing a sustained human presence on the lunar surface will require reliable and cost-effective access to life support consumables, particularly oxygen and water. While in-situ resource utilization (ISRU) has historically been evaluated for large-scale propellant production, early lunar habitation, such as the initial habitat concepts supporting the National Aeronautics and Space Administration’s (NASA’s) Moon Base program, represents a near-term and comparatively underexplored customer. This work presents a lifecycle cost–based methodology to estimate the normalized value of lunar-derived oxygen and water for an early habitation customer, expressed as the avoided lifecycle cost of Earth-based consumable resupply per kilogram delivered to the lunar surface. Leveraging assumptions that reflect initial Moon Base habitation concepts, mission architectures, and logistics paradigms, consumable demand is modeled and translated into delivered mass accounting for containment and packaging overhead. Lifecycle costs are estimated using multiple parametric cost estimating approaches and compared against representative pilot-scale ISRU system concepts to evaluate oxygen only, water only, and combined production architectures. Results emphasize that Earth-based consumable resupply is highly inefficient for early habitation, driven primarily by containment and packaging mass penalties. Oxygen exhibits values more than twice that of water on a per-kilogram basis despite lower demand b

title: Theory of the Alien
summary: Book developing a political theory of the Space Age through the figure of the alien, astropolitics and spacepower.
abstract: Theory of the Alien: Astropolitics, Spacepower, and the Outside develops a political theory of the Space Age organized around the conceptual figure of the alien, arguing that the constitution of outer space as an economic and warfighting domain transforms the categories through which we think politics and the human. Staging critical encounters with Helmuth Plessner, Carl Schmitt, Hans Blumenberg, and Bernard Stiegler, the book defines the astropolitical as the condition in which politics exceeds its terrestrial horizon, then derives a tentacular theory of spacepower in which orbital infrastructures reconfigure territory, perception, and strategy. Reading the mythopoetics of spaceflight, the conceptual history of ufology, and the UAP security crisis as sites where political theory discloses itself as political anthropology, it directs attention back to the planetary conditions of human life. Because those conditions are mediated rather than given, the book develops a planetary mythotechnics: an account of how strategic myths (from Homer to Cordwainer Smith) and technical infrastructures render the planet available to political contestation. Ultimately, only a traversal of the Outside and encountering what is alien can enable the rediscovery of the human. It will be essential reading for scholars and students in political theory, political geography, philosophical anthropology, science and technology studies, security studies, space policy, astroculture, and the environmental h

title: They Who Wield the Stars: How Privatization of the Space Industry is Transforming Global Politics
summary: Dissertation arguing privatisation of the space industry is a structural shift in power distribution in international politics.
abstract: The privatization of the space industry represents a significant structural shift in the distribution of power in the international political system. The Cold War space race was dominated by governmental agencies, but the new space race innovation is being run by private firms. These firms dominate launch services, support the world’s satellite communications, cloud infrastructure, surveillance, and other strategic infrastructure. This thesis asks: how is the privatization of the space industry transforming global politics? Conducting a comparative case study between the United States and China, this thesis demonstrates that the privatization of space is transforming global politics through three consecutive mechanisms: Super-Dependence, Consolidation, and Exposure. First, Super-Dependency describes how space is enabling several government and civilian infrastructures through just a few sectors, creating acute structural leverage. Second, Consolidation describes how the concentration of structural leverage to a few monopoly-holding firms increases their autonomy and bargaining power. Thirdly, Exposure describes how the private ownership of space-based strategic capabilities by actors who are not only profit-seeking but also have strong political preferences creates means and motive for tech billionaires to influence politics.

title: Three Origins and a Contemporary Projection: An Economic Genealogy of Space-Based Solar Power
summary: Builds an economic genealogy of the space-based solar power concept from its origins to the present.
abstract: The article attempts to construct a unified economic framework for analyzing the evolution of the space-based solar power (SBSP) concept. The study shows that the genealogy of SBSP can be represented as a three-part structure in which economic motives embedded in three intellectual traditions intertwine. The first of these — the Russian planetary school of the early 20th century (V.I. Vernadsky, B. Weinberg) — viewed cosmic energy as a resource for developing new territories and overcoming energy and resource constraints. The second tradition traces back to the literary-engineering image created by A. Asimov (1941), where the task of reducing transaction costs through the creation of capital-intensive, long-lived assets in orbit was first intuitively formulated. The third tradition is associated with the scientific systematization of N.S. Kardashev (1964), who linked the level of energy consumption with civilizational development, thereby giving a macroeconomic dimension to the issue under discussion. Until now, these three motives have typically been considered separately, and the task of their synthesis has not yet been explicitly posed. The novelty of the research also lies in introducing into scientific circulation the latest data from 2025–2026. This refers to projected LCOE values for the British Space Solar project by 2040, SpaceX’s application to create orbital data centers — positioned as a significant step for humanity towards achieving the planetary level (Type I)

title: Timeline of private spaceflight
Titan's Resources and their Utilization
summary: Preprint on Titan's resources and their utilization.
abstract: Saturn's moon Titan is a unique environment in the solar system. It is the only moon with an atmosphere, composed primarily of the gases N2 and CH4. It is also the only world to have abundant surface hydrocarbons CxHy, which are found as both liquids (seas, lakes) and solids (dunes). Meanwhile, oxygen is also readily accessible in the form of crustal water. This combination of abundant reduced carbon, along with available nitrogen and oxygen makes Titan an enticing world rich in resources that can be readily used to make food, fuel, building materials and more - potentially mission-enabling for long-duration voyages or habitats in the outer solar system. At the same time Titan, as an icy moon, is likely to be depleted at the surface in heavier elements including metals, which must therefore be found and brought from elsewhere. In this article we describe both the available resources on Titan, and also their potential uses. We compare and contrast the resource availability and potential in-situ utilization (ISRU) with other destinations suggested for human habitation such as the Moon and Mars. We conclude by discussing what future work will be important to further characterize Titan's resources, and to develop technologies for their utilization.

title: Toward a future space-based, highly scalable AI infrastructure system design
summary: Explores a scalable space-based compute system tapping solar power for future AI infrastructure.
abstract: The sun is the largest energy source in our solar system, and thus it warrants consideration how future AI infrastructure could most efficiently tap into that power. We explore a scalable compute system for machine learning (ML) in space: fleets of satellites equipped with solar arrays, free-space optics inter-satellite links, and Google tensor processing unit (TPU) accelerator chips. To facilitate high-bandwidth, low-latency inter-satellite communication, the satellites would be flown in close proximity. We illustrate the basic approach to formation flight via an 81-satellite cluster of 1 km radius and describe an approach for high-precision ML-enhanced models to control large-scale constellations. Trillium TPUs are radiation tested. They survive a total ionizing dose equivalent to a 5 year mission life without permanent failures and are characterized for bit-flip errors. Launch is critical to overall system cost; a learning curve analysis suggests launch to low-Earth orbit (LEO) may reach ≤$200/kg by mid-2030s.

title: Toward modeling principles for space energy system optimization
summary: Reviews energy system modelling studies and assesses their transferability to space to establish modelling principles for space energy optimization.
abstract: With the aim of establishing modeling principles for space energy system optimization, this paper systematically reviews existing energy system modeling studies and assesses their transferability to extraterrestrial environments. Core concepts from terrestrial energy system modeling, including technology selection, capacity expansion, sector coupling, and storage optimization, provide a valuable foundation. However, space applications require adaptations to account for material and commodity flows, thermodynamic constraints, demand structures and mission criticality, and substantial uncertainty in technology performance, resource availability, and environmental conditions. These challenges highlight the need for stronger coupling between technology-level thermodynamic analyses and system-level optimization, explicit representation of mission-critical demands, and stochastic and other uncertainty-aware optimization approaches. Based on these findings, preliminary modeling principles and key directions for future methodological development are identified. To demonstrate their applicability, a lunar space village case study is developed for a sustained settlement over a one-year operational period. The optimized system combines nuclear power, solar photovoltaics, batteries, electrolyzers, and fuel cells, resulting in a levelized cost of electricity of approximately 7,800 EUR /MWh. This provides a first quantitative benchmark for future lunar energy infrastructures. Overall, the
